ABSTRACT NO. 1
ORAL HEALTH ASSESSMENT IN CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE (CKD) PATIENTS ON MAINTENANCE HAEMODIALYSIS
Akash Rana, Gurvanit Kaur Lehl, Palak Dudeja, Gurasis Sodhi
Department of Nephrology; Government Medical College and Hospital; Chandigarh; India
E-mail:
sanjaydcruz@gmail.com
BACKGROUND:
CKD is disease of global health concern causing significant morbidity and mortality in patients worldwide. CKD causes multisystem manifestations which have been extensively studied but one lesser talked about aspect is the oral health issues which arises from the disease activity and therapy as well. This might stem from the uremic milieu imbalances in calcium and mineral metabolism endocrine and immune dysfunction all of which can contribute to inadequate oral health. CKD can lead to reduced salivary production due to restrictions on fluid intake retrograde parotitis breathing through the mouth and acidosis. These factors lead to dry mouth and alterations in the sense of taste. Elevated levels of salivary phosphorus and decreased magnesium encourage the formation of dental calculus a marker of suboptimal oral health. Additionally gingivitis occurs more frequently resulting in gum bleeding and increased vulnerability. This can be attributed to insufficient oral hygiene compromised overall health a weakened immune system and the presence of inflammation. CKD patients also exhibit a higher prevalence of periodontal pockets and greater tooth mobility. This is attributed to CKD-mineral bone disease (MBD) causing loss of mandible and maxillary alveolar bone and weakening of the periodontal ligament responsible for tooth loss which in turn leads to alterations in body image. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of mortality in CKD patients due accelerated atherosclerosis in CKD patients resulting from chronic inflammation. Periodontitis has been found to be associated with increased cardiovascular mortality in these patients and it has been shown that periodontitis if managed effectively this can decrease cardiovascular mortality in these patients. Oral health problems also lead to masticatory problems contributing to malnutrition which further aggravates the morbidity in CKD patients. There have been studies conducted in CKD patients to determine oral health problems associated with CKD and its effect on overall outcome in these patients in western population but data about Indian subcontinent population is scarce. Furthermore even fewer studies have been done to assess oral health in CKD patients on maintenance hemodialysis in Indian population. So we conducted this study to better understand the effects CKD and hemodialysis therapy on oral health of patients in the context of Indian population.
AIMS OF THE STUDY:
This study is to assess the oral health status of CKD patients on maintenance hemodialysis.
METHODS:
It was a cross-sectional prospective observational study spanning 12 months conducted at a single center with patients enrolled from in and out-patient department. Inclusion criteria: Adults diagnosed with CKD on maintenance hemodialysis (CKD-5D). Exclusion: Age less than 18 years CKD patients not on hemodialysis (CKD-ND). Sample Size of 80 was decided based on prevalence of Oral health problems among CKD patients as reported in earlier studies assuming 95% Confidence level and 10% absolute precision. Based on above criteria 80 patients were enrolled for the study after taking informed consent. The selected patients were administered to a questionnaire and were also subjected to oral health examination by qualified dental surgeon in department of dentistry by using following tools- 1. WHO oral health questionnaire. Available at
https://apps.who.int/iris/rest/bitstreams/453131/retrieve
pages 111 to 114 2. WHO oral health assessment form 2013 to look at various aspects of oral health such as dentition status periodontal status loss of attachment gingival bleeding dental erosion and oral mucosal lesions. Available at
https://apps.who.int/iris/rest/bitstreams/453131/retrieve
pages 83 and 84 The oral health symptoms were judged in four categories of tooth/mouth pain dry mouth mastication problems and body image issues based on the answers given to WHO oral health questionnaire. The oral health examination was used to assess four parameters: (1) Total number of sound teeth (2) DMFT score (decayed missing due to caries fixed tooth) which was used to assess the burden of caries. (3) Gingival bleeding score was used as marker of gingival health (4) Periodontitis was assessed based on clinical loss of attachment at site of greatest loss radiographic bone loss tooth loss due to periodontitis and probing depth. The results obtained from above study were then compared with data from similar study conducted previously at our center on CKD patients not on dialysis to determine the differences between two groups.
CONCLUSION:
(1) A comparison of results with a previous study conducted in our center which assessed oral health in CKD patients not on dialysis reveals an association between disease progression and increase in oral health problems with all parameters of oral health symptoms namely tooth/mouth pain, dry mouth, masticatory problems, and body image issues having statistically higher prevalence among CKD-5D group, (2) In the oral health examination, the DMFT score and Gingival bleeding score in CKD-5D group was higher than the CKD-ND group with p < 0.05 indicating statistically significant difference between dialysis and non-dialysis patients, (3) This data reveals increased burden of oral health problems in CKD-5D patients compared to CKD-ND patients indicating that oral disease burden increases with initiation of dialysis in CKD patients, (4) We suggest including oral health assessment on a periodic basis to look at this neglected aspect of poor oral health in CKD-5D which leads to poor nutrition, inflammation and body image issues, (5) Timely oral health assessment and management of dental issues will improve nutrition, reduce inflammation and provide a better quality of life to these patients.

ABSTRACT NO. 2
GENETIC ASSOCIATION IN PATIENTS WITH CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE OF UNKNOWN ETIOLOGY: AN OBSERVATIONAL STUDY
Tarun Kumar, A K Bhalla, Ratna Dua Puri, VaibhavÂ Tiwari
Department of Nephrology; Sir Ganga Ram Hospital; New Delhi; India
E-mail:
tarun.shikarwar@gmail.com
BACKGROUND:
Chronic kidney disease of unknown etiology is common and poses a substantial problem for patients in final management. We aim to utilize next generation sequencing in a single center to discover the genetic association in patients with Chronic Kidney Disease of unknown etiology.
AIMS OF THE STUDY:
To determine the diagnostic yield of whole exome sequencing in patients with Chronic Kidney Disease of unknown etiology.
METHODS:
In this observational cross-sectional study all the patients with chronic kidney disease of unknown etiology irrespective of age and gender were included. Clinical indications for genetic testing were categorized as glomerular diseases nephrolithiasis tubulopathies cystic kidney diseases chronic kidney disease of unknown etiology and others. Next genration sequencing was used for genetic analysis. The pathogenicity of the genetic variant was interpreted as per the American College of Medical genetics classification.
CONCLUSION:
Nearly one third (26.78%) of the patients with chronic kidney disease of unknown etiology underwent gene study and were tested positive for a genetic disease. Genetic testing confirmed the clinical diagnosis, changed the clinical diagnosis or made a new diagnosis, which helped in making better treatment strategies for the patients.

ABSTRACT NO. 3
TO STUDY THE PATTERN OF USE AND TOLERABILITY TO USE OF ACE INHIBITORS AND ARBS IN CKD PATIENTS WITH PROTEINURIC ILLNESS AND/OR CARDIAC FAILURE
Mahak Joshi, Gaurav Singla, Vikas Makkar
Department of Nephrology; DMCH; Ludhiana; Punjab; India
E-mail:
mahakg21@gmail.com
BACKGROUND:
Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE Inhibitors) and Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) are the best-studied antihypertensive agents that provide significant renal and cardiovascular protection for chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients. Recent studies suggest lack of evidence regarding the risk-benefit balance of ACE inhibitors/ARBs in patients with advanced CKD leading to their underutilization. There is need to assess the gap in the prescription and tolerability to use of these agents.
AIMS OF THE STUDY:
To study the Pattern of use and tolerability to use of ACE inhibitors and ARBs in CKD Patients with proteinuric illness and/or cardiac failure.
METHODS:
We conducted a prospective observational study on CKD Stage 3 & 4 patients. The study screening involved the eligible population. Out of eligible population only 33% patients were taking either ACE inhibitors or ARBs at the time of enrolment and remaining 67% patients were the new patients those who were started on ACE inhibitors or ARBs as a part of their treatment at the time of their enrolment into the study. Pattern for use of these drugs was studied and both these group of patients were followed for a period of 6 months to evaluate the tolerability to these drugs and to study the factors causing discontinuation among these patients.
CONCLUSION:
Our study reveals the underutilization of ACE inhibitors/ARBs in CKD patients with proteinuric illness and heart failure. Percentages of patients tolerating these medications were greater as compared to prevalence for their use for intended benefit. Tolerability of patients can be improved by a system of care that ensures regular checks of renal and cardiovascular function.

ABSTRACT NO. 4
SPECTRUM OF CLINICAL AND BIOCHEMICAL PROFILE OF TUBERCULOSIS IN PATIENTS WITH CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE AT TERTIARY CARE CENTER OF SOUTH INDIA-SINGLE CENTRE CROSS SECTIONAL OBSERVATIONAL STUDY
H A Karthik Urala, Avinash Thakur, Shweta S Phadke, Lalit Kumar Dasale, Ravitej Madipalli, Sree Bhushan Raju
Department of Nephrology; Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences; Hyderabad; Telangana; India
E-mail:
karthikurala@outlook.com
BACKGROUND:
Tuberculosis (TB) is among the most common causes of death from infectious disease worldwide. It is a s is major health illness in developing countries especially India. Immunodeficiency in CKD may make people moe vulnerable for TB. This study will focus on spectrum of clinical profile various organ involvement and outcome in Chronic Kidney Disease patients affected with Tuberculosis.
AIMS OF THE STUDY:
To study clinical profile of patients with chronic kidney disease diagnosed with Tuberculosis.
METHODS:
In the present study entitled Spectrum of clinical and biochemical profile of tuberculosis in patients with chronic kidney disease at tertiary care center of south India-single centre cross sectional observational study Study design-Cross sectional descriptive observational study Study setting: Department of Nephrology in a Tertiary Care Hospital in South India Study duration: 3 months after IEC approval Sample size:100 Study procedure The study was conducted after approval of the NIMS institutional ethics committee (NIEC). This study was a cross sectional observational study designed to be conducted Chronic Kidney Disease patients at NIMS hospital Hyderabad. Patients baseline medical records of CKD noted and data was collected from those who satisfy inclusion and exclusion criteria. Details like age sex demography presenting symptoms examination findings necessary investigations treatment details and other necessary information pertaining to the study was be collected. After inclusion routine investigations included complete blood picture and anemia workup blood chemistry analysis liver function tests ESR CRP TST and viral markers biochemical and microbiological fluid analysis reports were collected and Radiological imaging (Radiograph CT imaging) findings including nuclear scan reports such as FDG PET CT were noted. In selected patients histopathological examination reports were also noted Cases were defined 1. Sputum smear/CB NAAT /culture positive for M tuberculosis 2. Specimens positive for culture or CB NAAT for M tuberculosis 3. Radiologically proven Tuberculosis 4. Histopathological specimen showing necrotizing caseating granuloma All cases were treated for tuberculosis with ATT adjusted for weight and eGFR Duration of therapy is left to discretion of Physician or Nephrologist All patients were followed up for complications of ATT and at the end outcomes were noted.
CONCLUSION:
(1) Relative frequency of Tuberculosis in ESKD patients was high in our population, (2) Patients na ve to Renal Replacement Therapy (within 12 months) are at high risk of acquiring tuberculosis, (3) There is a high frequency of extra pulmonary TB. Therefore, a high index of suspicion for early diagnosis and treatment is required, (4) Microbiological diagnosis is seldom possible thus have to rely on clinical and radiological diagnosis.

ABSTRACT NO. 5
COMPARATIVE STUDY ON OUTCOME IN LIVING DONOR ABO INCOMPATIBLE AND PAIRED KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION
Neethu Varghese, Benil Hafeeq
1
, Jyothis Gopinathan
2
Departments of Nephrology and
2
IQRAA International Hospital and Research Centre; Kozhikode; Kerala; India
E-mail:
neethu7v@gmail.com
BACKGROUND:
The main obstacles for living donor transplantation are immunological incompatibility due to the presence of antibodies directed against the human leukocyte antigen system of the donor or due to the incompatibility of the ABO blood group system. Desensitization of recipient to remove the antibodies in order to prevent their rebound after transplantation and the exchange of organs between two or more donor recipient pairs are methods usually adopted to overcome the aforementioned problems. We aimed to compare the outcomes of paired exchange kidney transplantation with ABO incompatible kidney transplantation in our setting.
AIMS OF THE STUDY:
To compare the outcomes of paired exchange kidney transplantation with ABO incompatible kidney transplantation in our setting.
METHODS:
A review of medical records of 90 patients who underwent ABO incompatible transplantation and 46 patients who underwent paired kidney exchange from July 2016 to January 2023 was done. The patient’s demographics native kidney disease graft function at 6 months biopsy proven acute rejection incidence of delayed graft function need for dialysis following transplantation and patient survival were compared.
CONCLUSION:
The outcomes of paired kidney donation and ABO incompatible transplantations were comparable in terms of graft function at 6 months, biopsy proven acute rejections, delayed graft function and graft survival. Therefore, paired kidney donation and ABO incompatible donations should be encouraged in patients who has immunological incompatibility due to the presence of donor specific antigens.

ABSTRACT NO. 6
RIGHT VENTRICULAR DYSFUNCTION IN DIALYSIS PATIENTS
Rajinder Parshad, Jasmine Dass
Department of Nephrology; Government Medical College; Tanda; Himachal Pradesh; India
E-mail:
abhinavrana2729@gmail.com
Cardiovascular disease is leading cause of mortality in patients undergoing dialysis accounting 50% of deaths. Most of the available studies have focused on LV function in dialysis patients. In recent years the assessment of right ventricular function by tissue Doppler imaging (TDI) has been established as a common approach to detect preclinical abnormalities of cardiac function and has also been proposed as a reliable predictor of prognosis. Data on the prevalence of RVD in patients undergoing chronic dialysis are still lacking. A few studies that have investigated the impact of haemodialysis (HD) on RV functions have reported deterioration of RV systolic and diastolic functions in HD patients and very few have studied the impact on peritoneal dialysis patients. Importantly RVD may also affect left ventricular filling via interventricular interaction.
The aim of the study was to study the prevalence of right ventricular dysfunction in dialysis patients and to compare the impact of haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis on right ventricular dysfunction.
This prospective observational study was conducted in CKD - 5D patients in a tertiary care hospital in North India. Patients on haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis were included in the study. HD patients were further divided into two categories dialysis through radio-cephalic and through brachiocephalic fistula. All patients aged ≥ 18 years on haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis for at least 3 months were included. Haemodialysis patients receiving at least two sessions of dialysis/week and peritoneal dialysis patients with minimum 3 exchanges /day. Dialysis data regarding vascular access volume status and adequacy of dialysis was recorded. ECHO was done post dialysis (within one day of dialysis) by a trained technician or a doctor. In all patients evaluation of both RV and LV function was done by M -mode 2D and Doppler echocardiography by using ECHO machine SIEMENS ACUSON SC2000 with 4V1c transducer with a frequency of 3.5 MH in the left lateral and supine position. All measurements were performed according to the recommendations of the American Society of Echocardiography Recommendations 2015. Sample size was 52 quantitative variables were expressed as mean or median with standard deviation or interquartile range. Qualitative variables were expressed as frequency of occurrence with percentages. Appropriate statistical test such as Mann Whitney U test ‘U’ test and “chi square test” was used whenever required. A value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Right ventricular dysfunction was assessed using four ECHO parameters Tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE). Values lower than 17 mm are highly suggestive of RV systolic dysfunction. Right ventricular index of myocardial performance (RIMP). A RIMP greater than 0.54 by TDI is indicative of RV dysfunction. Tricuspid annular motion was evaluated by tissue Doppler to measure the longitudinal velocity of the tricuspid annulus. Velocity has been named the RV S’ or systolic excursion velocity. Normal values for pulsed tissue Doppler S wave is 14.1 ± 2.3 or >9.5 cm/s. The RV fractional area change (FAC) provides an estimate of global RV systolic function. Normal RV FAC is greater than 35%.
Of 56 patients included in the study 38 (67.9%) were male and 18 (32.1%) were female. Among 56 patients 44 (78.6%) patients had RVDD with any of the four factors positive while 12 (21.4%) had no dysfunction. TAPSE <17 mm was seen 19 (33.9%) patients while 37 (66.1%) patients had no RVDD suggested by TAPSE >17mm. RV FAC <35% was seen in 5 (8.9%) patients while 51 (91.1%) patients had RV FAC > 35% suggestive of no dysfunction. 29 (51.8%) patients had RVDD characterised by RIMP >0.54 while 27 (48.2%) patients had RIMP < 0.54 suggestive of no dysfunction. S PRIME < 9.5cm/s was seen in 10 (17.9%) patients which was suggestive of RVDD and 46 (82.1%) patients had S PRIME > 9.5cm/s suggestive of no RVDD dysfunction. On comparing ECHO parameters between HD and PD group the average LV Ejection fraction in Haemodialysis group was 44.34 Â± 10.82% and Peritoneal dialysis group was 53.07 ± 8.11% and the difference was statistically significant (p<0.05). Among the four parameters for Right ventricular dysfunction TAPSE, RVFAC, RIMP and S-Prime, TAPSE <17 mm was found in 17 (41.5%) HD patients and only 2 (13.3%) peritoneal dialysis patient and was statistically significant (p < 0.05) rest all other ECHO parameters of RV dysfunction showed no significant statistical difference.
RVD assessment is of paramount significance in patients undergoing dialysis as RVD is present in large number of patients undergoing dialysis. The prevalence of RVD was 78.6%. The prevalence is higher in HD group compared to PD group (87.8 vs 53.3%, p < 0.05). Moreover, while assessing RVD all the four parameters for measuring RVD TAPSE, RIMP, RVFAC, should be measured as this increases the sensitivity of detecting RVD. Further we can conclude that PD can be considered as a better dialysis modality as far as RVD is concerned but whether it relates to morbidity or mortality is not evaluated in this study.

ABSTRACT NO. 7
IS GENETIC ANALYSIS ACTUALLY NECESSARY IN A DEVELOPING COUNTRY? - “ ANALYSIS OF SPECTRUM OF MUTATIONS IN PATIENTS WITH NEPHROTIC SYNDROME
Harrini Devi Palani Baskar, Prathiba Parthasarathy, Gopikumar Sekar, Dinesh Kumar Thanigachalam, Jayalakshmi Seshadri, Natarajan Gopalakrishnan
Department of Nephrology; Madras Medical College; Chennai; Tamil Nadu; India
E-mail:
harrinidevi@gmail.com
BACKGROUND:
Genetic screening as a part of nephrotic syndrome work-up is well established in developed countries. In developing countries like India the role of genetic screening is not clearly established because of financial constraints. There is no clear guidelines for weaning of immunosuppression in SRNS patients without genetic analyses.
AIMS OF THE STUDY:
To study the prevalence of genetic mutations among challenging nephrotic syndrome patients and its usefulness in weaning of immunosuppressive therapy.
METHODS:
We have retrospectively analysed 34 nephrotic syndrome patients, genetic analyses done from Jan 2022 to July 2023 at Institute of Nephrology Madras Medical College. Genetic analyses were done using Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS) and patients were analysed for targeted nephrotic syndrome panel and some were supplemented with whole exome sequencing. Patients demographic data pattern of nephrotic syndrome reason for genetic analyses clinical presentation association of syndromic features presence or absence of mutation associated with nephrotic syndrome and renal biopsy findings were analysed. Statistical analyses were done using SPSS version 23.
CONCLUSION:
An unequivocal molecular diagnosis could allow us for framing a personalised treatment approach with reduction or stopping of immunosuppressive therapy, avoidance of renal biopsy and provision of genetic counselling and recurrence risk assessment post renal transplant. Identification of new causative mutations will help us to discover new pathogenic mechanisms of glomerular disease and provide new insights into podocyte biology, glomerular function and mode of treatment for nephrotic syndrome.

ABSTRACT NO. 8
COMPARATIVE STUDY ON DIETARY PATTERN AND KNOWLEDGE ATTITUDE PRACTICE (KAP) DURING PRE AND POST DIETARY INTERVENTION AMONG DIFFERENT STAGES OF CKD PATIENTS
Deepshikha Khattar, Lakshman, Muthu Kumar, Himansu Sekhar Mahapatra
Department of Nephrology; Atal Bihari Vajpayee Institute of Medical Sciences and Dr. RML Hospital; New Delhi; India
E-mail:
deepshikhakhattar@gmail.com
BACKGROUND:
KAP assessment on dietary habits and patterns have emerged as a practical approach to evaluate qualitative as well as quantitative management aspects of CKD. However scanty data is available on the KAP of dietary habits and effect of change in dietary pattern after counselling.
AIMS OF THE STUDY:
Comparison of dietary pattern and knowledge attitude practice (KAP) and effect of dietary habits after dietary counselling among different stages of CKD patients.
METHODS:
In this one-year study patients of CKD 3 to 5 (ND) of age 18 to 60 years were enrolled from nephrology OPD. Basic demographic profile socio- economic status dietary habits and physical activity details are being recorded. Normal subjects were also taken for comparison and their dietary nutrient analysis (calories protein sodium potassium calcium phosphorus liquid) was done by Diet Cal version 10.0 software using a 4-day dietary record. Dietary nutrients and nutritional status were measured at baseline and every 6 months for only CKD patients. Patients were categorised into Normal protein (0.8-1.0 gm/kg/day) low protein (0.6 gm/kg/day) and very low protein (0.3 gm/kg/day) categories. Knowledge Attitude and practice was also recorded at baseline and after 6 months. All patients underwent dietary intervention with a home-based PS diet. Dietary re-enforcement and counselling for clinical as well as diet-related patient concerns were done by exclusive renal dieticians with weekly telephone calls. All the parameters were analysed by using the Chi-Square test paired/unpaired t-tests and one-way ANOVA to assess Effect of PS.
CONCLUSION:
Study showed a significant increase in knowledge, attitude and practice at one year after dietary counselling. Further, there were significant changes in intake of energy, protein, fats, carbohydrates, potassium, phosphorus and progression in all stages of CKD.

ABSTRACT NO. 9
THROMBOTIC MICROANGIOPATHIES POST RENAL TRANSPLANTATION
Ajey Indrajeet Jha, Umapati Hegde, Sishir Gang, Mohan Rajapurkar, Abhijit Konnur, Hardik Patel
Department of Nephrology; Muljibhai Patel Society for Research in Nephro-Urology; Nadiad; Gujarat; India
E-mail:
ajeyjha@gmail.com
BACKGROUND:
Thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) is a life-threatening disease characterized by endothelial dysfunction and presence of platelet thrombi in small blood vessels causing thrombocytopenia and causing microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. TMA is a serious complication affecting kidney transplant recipients in 0.8–14% of patients leading to poor graft and patient survival. It can either occur in a systemic form or renal limited TMA either occur as a recurrent disease or de Novo with later being more common. Post Transplant TMA can be caused by complement protein mutations drug induced Antibody mediated rejection infections. Patients improved with treatment of the etiological agent plasma exchange which usually improve the hematological abnormality or complement blockade with eculizumab.
AIMS OF THE STUDY:
Our aim was to study the graft outcomes after TMA in Renal transplant recipients.
METHODS:
This was a single centre Retrospective cohort study where 64 renal transplant recipients who developed biopsy proven TMA out of the 766 renal transplant done at our centre from Jan 2017 to Dec 2022. Data collected included demographic parameter creatinine Complete blood count and histopathology. Graft outcomes were defined based on the serum creatinine at last follow up.
CONCLUSION:
TMA in the post transplant period is commonly associated with drug toxicities, ABMR, or recurrent HUS. There is no correlation between drug levels and extent or prognosis of TMA. Change of CNI, Plasma exchange however remains the mainstay of the treatment.

ABSTRACT NO. 10
INSIGHT INTO CLINICAL AND PATHOLOGICAL PERSPECTIVES OF RENAL ALLOGRAFT DYSFUNCTION: A 10-YEAR EXPERIENCE
V R Krishnakumar, T P Noushad
1
, R Sajeevkumar
1
, Noble Gracious
1
, Vineetha
1
Departments of Nephrology and
1
Government Medical College; Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala; India
E-mail:
krishnakumarvylapally@gmail.com
BACKGROUND:
Renal allograft dysfunction remains a significant challenge in kidney transplantation as highlighted by a decade-long single-center experience. The complexity and impact of this issue stem from a diverse range of native kidney diseases and donor characteristics emphasizing the need for personalized management strategies. Detecting problems early and implementing targeted interventions are vital for improving graft survival and patient well-being. To enhance transplant protocols and patient care further research and collaboration are essential with the aim of achieving better graft outcomes in the future. Additionally exploring the potential of NLR and Banff scores in multicenter studies can provide deeper insights into their role in understanding and managing renal allograft dysfunction.
AIMS OF THE STUDY:
Characterize Clinicopathological Profiles of kidney transplant recipients experiencing allograft dysfunction including demographic data transplantation history and clinical presentations. Correlate Clinical Data with Biopsy Findings: Analyze renal biopsy results and correlate them with clinical data including immunosuppressive regimens donor information Identify Underlying Causes: Determine the underlying causes of renal allograft dysfunction in the study population distinguishing between rejection infection drug toxicity and other factors.
METHODS:
This retrospective single-center study was conducted at Government Medical College Thiruvananthapuram focusing on renal allograft biopsies spanning from 2012 to 2023 as documented in the department records. To ensure the completeness of our dataset missing data from these biopsies were meticulously collected through a combination of telephone inquiries and patient visits to the Transplant Outpatient Department (OPD). This comprehensive approach allowed us to compile a robust and detailed dataset providing a solid foundation for our analysis of renal allograft dysfunction over the specified timeframe.
CONCLUSION:
Renal allograft dysfunction remains a significant challenge in kidney transplantation, as highlighted by a decade-long single-center experience. The complexity and impact of this issue stem from a diverse range of native kidney diseases and donor characteristics, emphasizing the need for personalized management strategies. Detecting problems early and implementing targeted interventions are vital for improving graft survival and patient well-being. To enhance transplant protocols and patient care, further research and collaboration are essential, with the aim of achieving better graft outcomes in the future. Additionally, exploring the potential of NLR and Banff scores in multicenter studies can provide deeper insights into their role in understanding and managing renal allograft dysfunction.

ABSTRACT NO. 11
CLINICOPATHOLOGICAL PROFILE AND HEMATO-RENAL OUTCOMES OF LARGEST BIOPSY COHORT OF RENAL AMYLOIDOSIS FROM SOUTH ASIA
Rizwan Alam, Elenjickal Elias John, Sanjeet Roy, Selvin Sundar Raj, Joseph Johny, Manish Lalwani, Nisha Jose, Sabina Yusuf, Jeethu Joseph Eapen, Athul Thomas, Vinoi George David, Santosh Varughese, Suceena Alexander
Department of Nephrology; CMC; Vellore; Tamil Nadu; India
E-mail:
rizwangb0557@gmail.com
Kidney is the most common organ involved in systemic amyloidosis. This study reports the clinicopathological outcomes of the largest series of renal amyloidosis from South Asia.
To study the Clinicopathological Profile and Hemato-renal Outcomes of renal amyloidosis in a tertiary care centre from South Asia.
This retrospective biopsy registry cohort included 260 consecutive patients of renal amyloidosis who underwent kidney biopsy between January 2005 to December 2022 at our tertiary care hospital in South India.
The mean age of the cohort was 52.5 ± 11.3 years and 175/260 (67.3%) were males. The type of amyloid was immunoglobulin (Ig) amyloidosis in 190 (73.1%), AA amyloidosis in 40 (15.4%) and unclassified in 30 (11.5%) patients. AL was the predominant type of Ig amyloidosis (186/190, 97.9%). Extrarenal involvement was seen in 59 (22.7%) patients. The most involved extrarenal organs were cardiovascular (42/260, 16.1%) and gastrointestinal (14/260, 5.4%) system. Rheumatological diseases constituted the commonest etiology of AA amyloidosis (20/40, 50%). Patients of Ig amyloidosis had more proteinuria [5.1 (IQR, 3.2-7.2) versus 3.7 (IQR, 1.9-8.1) g/day] but higher eGFR [68.2 (IQR, 35.9-100.3) versus. 28.4 (IQ R, 17.3-59.8) ml/min/1.73 m] than patients with AA amyloidosis at presentation. Among the patients of Ig amyloidosis, M band on electrophoresis was seen in 78/90 (86.7%), abnormal IFE in 93/165 (56.4%), abnormal kappa: lambda ratio in 99/165 (60%) and 24.2 % (46/190) patients met the criteria of multiple myeloma. Amyloid deposits were seen universally within the glomeruli; 206/260 (79.2%) and 88/260 (33.8%) had additional vascular and interstitial deposits. Forty-one percent (104/290) received RAAS inhibitors and 73% of patients with Ig amyloidosis received CyBorD chemotherapy regimen. Of the 116 patients with follow-up details more than 3 months, 21(18.1%) progressed to kidney failure, 86/98 (87.7%) had persistent proteinuria and 32/43 (74.4%) patients of Ig amyloidosis attained a hematologic response VGPR. Only 1/32 (3.1%) patients who attained hematological response VGPR progressed to kidney failure. Sixteen patients (13.7%) died during the follow-up period due to infections and cardiovascular disease.
Majority of cases of renal amyloidosis are Ig derived. Attainment of VGPR is associated with better renal response.

ABSTRACT NO. 12
EXPANDING THE DONOR POOL IN RENAL TRANSPLANTATION: COMPARISON OF OUTCOME BETWEEN DECEASED DONOR PAIRED KIDNEY EXCHANGE AND ABO INCOMPATIBLE TRANSPLANTATION - SINGLE CENTER EXPERIENCE
Aparna Balachandran, Sajith Narayanan, N A Ismail, Feroz Aziz, B Sreejesh, A Thushara
Department of Nephrology; Aster MIMS Hospital; Kozhikode; Kerala; India
E-mail:
aparnabhay@gmail.com
BACKGROUND:
Transplant programs are forced to pursue ABO-incompatible (ABOiTX) and Paired kidney exchange (PKE) as the deceased donor program (DDKT) has been unpredictable. Immunological and logistic challenges of ABOiTX and PKE make it difficult to be done as routine.
AIMS OF THE STUDY:
We aim to compare the outcome of DDKT ABOiTX and PKE with respect to renal function incidence of acute rejections (AR) death censored graft survival (DCGS) and patient loss (PL).
METHODS:
Retrospective observational study from 2012 to 2022. We have reviewed the data of ABOiTX or PKE or DDKT from our institute during the study period. Incidence of AR Graft Loss (GL) or PL were compared.
CONCLUSION:
The long-term results show the feasibility of expanding donor options. PKE and ABOiTx have better graft survival compared to DDKT. PKE has better death censored graft survival compared to ABOiTx. PKE helps to transplant sensitized patients without increased risk of allograft AR. Better allocation criteria may help in improving DDKT outcomes.

ABSTRACT NO. 13
PROFILE OF RENAL RE-TRANSPLANTATION IN A TERTIARY CARE CENTER IN SOUTH INDIA: A SINGLE CENTRE EXPERIENCE.
Kiran Ravi, Kartik Ganesh, Jitin S Kumar, Sunita Simon, M Abi Abraham
VPS Lakeshore Hospital and Research Center; Kochi; Kerala; India
E-mail:
kiransark26@gmail.com
BACKGROUND:
Advances in immunosuppression have prolonged the life of renal allografts although not indefinitely. Acute organ shortage has lead to increasing demand for renal re-transplantation all over the world. Many studies report inferior outcomes compared to primary transplantation. The cause for inferior outcomes reported to be due to increased duration of dialysis after graft failure to retransplantation acute rejections vascular thrombosis infections smoking recipient age and comorbidities. BACKGROUND:

The most important non-traditional risk factor is abnormal mineral metabolism also known as chronic kidney disease mineral bone disorder (CKD-MBD). One of the key players in CKD-MBD is fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) a phosphaturic hormone and physiologic inhibitor of vitamin D secreted by the osteocytes. With declining kidney function serum phosphate level rises due to its decreased excretion. As a result FGF23 level also rises. Higher FGF23 levels have been shown to predispose to a higher risk of mortality. Multiple studies have demonstrated the independent association of higher levels of FGF23 with left ventricular hypertrophy. Arterial calcification an important mechanism of cardiovascular disease in CKD has inconsistent association with FGF23. Studies have shown that higher levels of FGF23 was associated with left ventricular hypertrophy reduced ejection fraction (EF) congestive heart failure events and cardiovascular mortality. An experimental study showed an inhibitory effect of FGF23 on erythropoiesis. However only a few human studies have suggested a possible association between FGF23 and anemia in CKD patients. Interestingly few animal and human studies showed that absolute and functional iron deficiencies stimulate FGF23 production. Studies are scarce in the Indian population. The only study on level of FGF23 in maintenance hemodialysis patients in India conducted in few hospitals in South India showed that FGF23 levels were significantly associated with serum phosphorus and parathyroid hormone levels and no significant association between FGF23 and cardiovascular comorbidities and mortality was shown.
AIM OF THE STUDY:
The aim of the study was to correlate levels of FGF23 with cardiovascular events in CKD patients on MHD.
METHODS:
This was a single-centre hospital based prospective study. It was conducted in the Dialysis unit of the Department of Nephrology in Advanced Medicare and Research Institute (AMRI) Dhakuria Kolkata. Adult patients (age >18 years) of either gender diagnosed to have end stage renal disease (ESRD) on maintenance haemodialysis (MHD) of duration at least 3 months attending Dialysis unit of AMRI Dhakuria were included. Patients below age of 18 years those with early CKD patients with history of cardiovascular disease prior to diagnosis of CKD and patients with history of any type of anemia prior to diagnosis of CKD were excluded. Eight patients were lost to follow up and 14 patients did not have all the necessary data for analysis. So the final analysis included 50 patients. From each of the patients 4 ml of blood was obtained in clot vial by nursing staff of the dialysis unit from their HD access just prior to the beginning of their hemodialysis. The samples were stored in -80 degree Celsius after centrifugation. After all the samples were collected the test for FGF23 level using a standard ELISA kit from Elabscience was conducted in the month of March 2020. Patients were then followed up for 16 months i.e till June 2021. They were interviewed and information regarding demographic data such as age and sex along with history of other comorbidities such as hypertension diabetes hypothyroidism ischemic heart disease cerebrovascular disease or neurological disorders were obtained. They were asked about their dialysis history- like duration of dialysis frequency of dialysis per week vascular access etc. A detailed medication history was also obtained. A thorough physical examination was conducted. All the data collected were analysed for correlation with FGF23 level.
CONCLUSION:
In the present study, Higher levels of FGF23 were found to be associated with left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) and evidence of left ventricular strain. FGF23 levels also correlated with LV dysfunction as evidenced by a positive correlation with NT-proBNP. In the patient population, 26% developed heart failure. However, there was no statistically significant association between hemoglobin levels and FGF23 quartiles.

Later scoring systems used for other purposed like Lupus nephritis Banff classification of transplant pathology etc were used in AAV-GN. But since the clinical scenario had wide difference these were not widely accepted. In 2010 Berden et al. introduced the popular classification based on baseline glomerular involvement and its association with renal survival at 1 and 5 years. As it was confined to glomerular only -based classification it had its drawbacks. In 2018 a new clinico-pathologic score the Brix’s ANCA Renal Risk Score (RRS) was developed which took into consideration both clinical and histopathological factors. Similarly The Mayo Clinic Chronicity Score (MCCS) published in 2017 also takes into account glomerular tubular and vascular status for prognostication. Thus it is necessary to identify patients with higher stage for whom aggressive immunosuppressive therapy will be life saving.

Conversely for patients without ESKD the follow-up duration was defined as the period between AAV-GN diagnosis and the last visit. The clinical and biochemical variables collected include Age Sex Hb at diagnosis S. Cr at diagnosis eGFR at diagnosis and Urine PC ratio at diagnosis. The histopathological variables assessed include- The class according to Berdens classification the extent of glomerular involvement (global or segmental) type of crescent presence of acute tubular injury interstitial inflammation interstitial fibrosis tubular atrophy fibrinoid necrosis intimal fibrosis/ hyperplasia arterial medial sclerosis and antibody status (Ig G Ig A Ig M C3 C1q Kappa and Lambda). All statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows version 26.0. Continuous variables were expressed as medians with interquartile ranges whereas categorical variables were expressed as numbers (percentages). Significant differences between two categorical variables were analysed using the chi-square and Fisher’s exact tests. The Mann Whitney U test was used to identify significant differences between two continuous variables. Comparisons of the cumulative ESKD-free and patients survival rates between the two groups were analysed using the Kaplan Meier survival analysis with log-rank tests. Statistical significance was set as P<0.05.
CONCLUSION:

Yet diagnosing genetic FSGS not only have implications for prognostication therapy transplantation but also for family and family planning. There are very few studies in India on factors affecting FSGS and the importance of genetic screening. There are no clinical or histopathological findings to distinguish genetic FSGS from other types. However there are several hallmarks of genetic disease a positive family history early age at disease onset severe/ steroid resistant disease. Over 50 genes responsible for FSGS have been identified. Furthermore in case of a living related transplantation it is safest to have a genetically unaffected family member as donor. Likewise advanced techniques such as pre-implantation genetic diagnosis can be used to prevent the inheritance of the disease to the future children of a genetic FSGS patient.

A structured questionnaire was used for data collection. It included details of socio demography clinical investigations histopathology treatment and course of the disease. Patients having any of the following indications were advised for genetic testing: presence of congenital/infantile onset of nephrotic syndrome presence of syndromic or extra renal features steroid resistant nephrotic syndrome or presence of positive family history. Although most cases of TTP are considered to be primary or idiopathic some cases have been reported to have a number of precipitating factors including malignancies immunological disorders toxic substances infectious agents and several medications (e.g. clopidogrel mitomycin ticlopidine quinine ticagrelor) and pregnancy. Of the medications ticlopidine ticagrelor and clopidogrel have been associated with TTP following coronary stenting. The greatest risk of developing life-threatening TTP has been reported to occur within 2 weeks after initiating drug. TTP is one of the dreaded but uncommon causes of thrombocytopenia and anemia. A clinical entity identical to classic TTP that rarely occurs postoperatively is called postoperative TTP and it occurs usually after 4-5 days of surgery. One should suspect it in a patient with normal hemoglobin preoperatively who subsequently develops MAHA and thrombocytopenia. The surgical procedures associated with pTTP include cardiac surgery such as CABG vascular surgery G.I surgery. In contrast to classical TTP the pentad of fever impaired renal function thrombocytopenia hemolyticanemia and altered mental status are usually not present making pTTP is a diagnosis of exclusion.
AIMS OF THE STUDY:
To highlight this rare case of Post PTRA TTP in an unusual case of vasculitis presenting as Bilateral renal artery thrombosis.

Patient was started on steroids anticoagulants continued haemodialysis and plan for renal artery stenting at later date.
